conventions.convention: Phase equivalence means U = λV with |λ| = 1; exact matrix equality retains every scalar phase.
A two-level block acts in the specified ordered pair (x,y), including its phase, and is identity on that pair's orthogonal complement.
Rotations use R_a(t) = exp(−itσ_a/2); R_y has negative upper-right and positive lower-left sine entries.
Controlled matrices use control-first order; C(λU) = (diag(1,λ) ⊗ I)C(U), so a target scalar becomes a relative control phase.

The generic lower bound assumes countable choice for normalized Frobenius volume; identification with Haar probability additionally assumes full AC. It is an almost-everywhere assertion with no ancillas.
Terminal diagonals migrate only through separators preserving every computational label on the same two slot wires; the final slot retains its three-CNOT allowance.
The Gray-path resource formulas count literal gate occurrences, retaining identity gates and using reversed adjoint lists for return swaps; clean workspace is returned after every call.
The optimized QSD formula applies for n ≥ 2; n = 1 needs no CNOT, and at n = 0 exact positive-arity circuit syntax realizes only the identity scalar.

load_bearing.statement: For every U ∈ U(2) there are real δ, α, θ, β with U = e^{iδ}R_z(α)R_y(θ)R_z(β). If det U = 1, the scalar factor is unnecessary.
For finite-dimensional complex H and unitary U₀,U₁ on H, diag(U₀,U₁) = (I ⊗ V)diag(D,D*)(I ⊗ W), for unitary V,W and diagonal unitary D.

For k ≥ 1 and U ∈ U(2k), there are block-diagonal unitaries L,R and nonnegative real diagonal C₀,S₀ with U = L[[C₀,−S₀],[S₀,C₀]]R, C₀² + S₀² = I, and 0 ≤ C₀,S₀ ≤ I. Singular values 0 and 1 are allowed.
Every U ∈ U(4) equals e^{iδ}(A ⊗ B)exp(i(aX ⊗ X + bY ⊗ Y + cZ ⊗ Z))(C ⊗ D), with A,B,C,D ∈ SU(2) and real a,b,c,δ.

Every U ∈ U(4) factors exactly as U = ΔV, where Δ is computational-basis diagonal and V has a no-ancilla circuit with at most two CNOTs and arbitrary one-qubit gates. For N slots on the same two wires separated by label-preserving operations, the slots cost at most 2(N−1)+3 CNOTs.
For r ≥ 1, an r-controlled X has an exact O(r) one-qubit/CNOT circuit with one additional borrowed wire; the complete circuit equals C^r(X) ⊗ I on the entire register, including entangled inputs.

Assume countable choice. For fixed n ≥ 1 and an m-CNOT skeleton with arbitrary exact one-qubit gates and no ancillas, its exact matrices lie in a finite union of smooth images of parameter spaces of dimension at most 3n+4m+1. If this is less than 4^n, the skeleton is volume-null; under full AC it is Haar-null.

For n ≥ 2, every n-qubit unitary has an exact no-ancilla circuit with arbitrary one-qubit gates and at most (23/48)4^n − (3/2)2^n + 4/3 CNOTs. The statement separately treats widths one and zero and asserts no decomposition-time or finite-precision bit-complexity bound.

concerns.concern: The Statement says the Frobenius metric induces 'a normalized volume probability μ_F' and that 'Its null sets are exactly the sets that are Lebesgue-null in these charts,' without stating AC_ω or specifying the measure domain. Facts A1 and Proof 6.1 explicitly require AC_ω and establish the criterion for Borel sets; both published measure suppliers distinguish their Borel measures from their completions. The Statement should carry the choice hypothesis and clarify whether its null-set assertion concerns Borel sets, completed sets, or outer-null sets. The geometric manifold assertion itself is unaffected.

seams_checked.note: Uses chronological products with later gates on the left, positive gate arity, explicit wire tuples, and occurrence-based resources. The zero-wire QSD case respects this syntax.
Controlled blocks, CNOT orientation, and phase corrections agree with the supplier definitions; controlled access is not inferred from ordinary black-box access.
Pauli Y signs and exp(−itσ/2) rotations agree throughout Euler, Gray-code, controlled-unitary, and three-CNOT calculations.
Ordered computational bases, big-endian encoding, first-argument-linear pairing, and the one-dimensional empty register are preserved.
Clean work bits return to zero for every data input; borrowed-wire constructions establish a full tensor-identity return, including correlated inputs.
The controlled-phase approximation theorem quotes the exact relative-phase identity and compiles a complete controlled block rather than controlling an uncorrected projective approximation.
Phase-equivalence uses retain explicit representatives in norm constraints; the Rz phase-reduction theorem quotes the controlled-phase identity faithfully.

This is a page-level prerequisite without a direct owned-item citation in its listed items. Its independent acceptance-phase proof and finite-description cost model respect the same phase and resource boundaries.

The local QSD existence proof uses cosine-sine, demultiplexing, and the three-CNOT base case without importing an efficiency claim. Its Euler conversion explicitly reverses angle signs, and width zero is treated at channel level.

Optimized QSD and multicontrol consumers preserve their gate models and width restrictions. Unoptimized routing uses its separate recurrence; the fixed-arity Cauchy decomposition hardcodes only fixed finite branch choices and does not claim general real-input zero testing.

Isometry synthesis applies QSD directly to the completed unitary times its input permutation, preserves the width-zero exception, and does not require output workspace to return clean. Fixed-arity compilation keeps arithmetic time separate from gate counts.
